title: Harder, better, faster, stronger, and with less annotated data: ESGAN and plant sciences
content: The era of big data for plant research is in full swing. From quantifying gene expression at the single-cell level to characterizing the complete plant metabolome, we now have a wealth of information to better understand plants. While such omics techniques have led the way in high-throughput data collection, we are witnessing a parallel rise in large-scale phenomics, truly revolutionizing how we perform plant research (Awada et al. 2024; Murphy et al. 2024). Using high-throughput phenotyping tools, growth, stress, and phenology can be monitored with high temporal and spatial resolution and with less human labor. These tools are applied for the screening of germplasm collections, informing breeding strategies, investigating agronomic traits, and assisting in decision-making in labs, fields, or in larger agricultural systems. Nevertheless, this transformation brings new challenges as well. Handling and interpreting such large volumes of data can be complex and resource intensive. In this regard, the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods has been a true game-changer (Murphy et al. 2024).
